subject.title: Days
subject.author: Philip Larkin
subject.text:
What are days for?
Days are where we live.   
They come, they wake us   
Time and time over.
They are to be happy in:   
Where can we live but days?

Ah, solving that question
Brings the priest and the doctor   
In their long coats
Running over the fields.

title: The Ending Larkin Didn't Know He'd Already Read
standfirst: In August 1953 Philip Larkin dashed off ten lines he called hardly a poem at all, then swapped out its ending before it ever reached Faber. Eighteen years later, rereading a book Monica Jones had given him one Christmas, he worked out by accident where that new ending had actually come from.

sections.heading: Hardly a Poem at All
sections.body:
Larkin finished "Days" on 3 August 1953, sub-librarian at Queen's University Belfast, three years into the job and three years into his relationship with Monica Jones, the Leicester lecturer he wrote to almost daily. Two days later he sent her the poem itself, introduced with no ceremony at all: ["I've written a tiny little poem" since returning](https://ripe-tomato.org/2013/05/13/more-on-days-by-larkin/), "hardly a poem at all." He signed off the same casually: "Don't take it seriously, but it's a change from the old style."

The change was real. Larkin's poems mostly rhyme and scan — *Church Going*, written the previous year, runs in tight seven-line stanzas. "Days" has neither rhyme nor regular metre; it reads closer to the [free-verse Imagists](https://interestingliterature.com/2016/11/a-short-analysis-of-philip-larkins-days/) of a generation before him than to anything else he was writing in 1953. He would use the same loose form again, in poems like *Water* and *Going* — but this was the first time, and he clearly didn't rate it. It sat unpublished for eleven years before Faber ran it in *The Whitsun Weddings* in 1964.

sections.heading: The Word Larkin Swapped In
sections.body:
The letter Larkin sent Monica did not carry the poem's final text. Its penultimate line originally read "And to seek where they join" — the priest and the doctor arriving, in that draft, because their two jurisdictions meet somewhere and someone has gone looking for the seam. [By the time it reached print, that line had become](https://ripe-tomato.org/2013/05/13/more-on-days-by-larkin/) "Ah, solving that question":

> Ah, solving that question
> Brings the priest and the doctor
> In their long coats
> Running over the fields.

The swap changes what the poem is afraid of. "Where they join" is an almost administrative image — two professions meeting at a boundary. "Solving that question" turns the whole opening stanza's cheerful "What are days for?" into a trap: answer it properly, finally, and you get a house call from death's two authorised representatives. One reader of the poem has argued that Larkin is setting a trap for anyone too satisfied with their own answer — that ["the hunger for a final answer may be a symptom, not a mark of wisdom."](https://jwikeley.substack.com/p/what-are-days-for) Not everyone reads it that darkly: the Philip Larkin Society's own commentary calls it ["a wilfully cheerful poem"](https://philiplarkin.com/poem-reviews/days-2/) that earns its sentiment rather than fakes it. Both readings depend on the same four rewritten words.

sections.heading: Eighteen Years to Notice
sections.body:
"Days" had been in print for seven years when, on 21 November 1971, Larkin sat down with an old favourite — Kenneth Grahame's *The Wind in the Willows* — and noticed something about his own poem. ["I was rereading The Wind in the Willows,"](https://ripe-tomato.org/2013/05/13/more-on-days-by-larkin/) he wrote to Monica, "& found within a few pages of each other 'long coats' and 'running' and 'over the fields'. Isn't that odd?" He traced it to chapter ten, *The Further Adventure of Toad*, and concluded he had lifted the phrasing without ever meaning to: "I'm sure I got the words from there — hiding places thirty years deep, at least."

Thirty years deep meant childhood. Larkin was born in 1922; a book he'd absorbed decades before he ever sat down to write about priests, doctors and days had apparently supplied the poem's closing image whole, and he hadn't recognised it until he happened to reread the source by chance, nearly two decades after publishing the poem it had furnished.

sections.heading: Two Scenes Welded Into One
sections.body:
The chapter Larkin named is Toad's car chase. Toad has stolen a motor and driven it into a horse-pond; [the men who tried to stop him are left](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Wind_in_the_Willows_%281908%29/Chapter_10) — this is the exact sentence — "encumbered by their long coats," "floundering helpless in the water." They are not running anywhere. A little further down the same page, Toad himself, alone, does the running: he "set off running across country as hard as he could, scrambling through hedges, jumping ditches, pounding across fields, till he was breathless and weary." He is not wearing a long coat.

So the single figure in Larkin's last two lines — someone in a long coat, running over a field — does not exist anywhere in Grahame's book. It is a splice: the coats belong to the drenched, stationary gentlemen; the running and the fields belong to the fleeing toad. Larkin's own letter says he found the phrases "within a few pages of each other," not in one sentence — which means the fusion happened in his memory, not on Grahame's page. What reads in "Days" as one grim detail, a matched pair of professionals hurrying to a deathbed, was assembled without his knowledge out of a comic chase scene involving neither death nor a doctor.

sections.heading: A Book for Rabbithood
sections.body:
The particular copy mattered. Monica Jones had given Larkin a [Rackham-illustrated edition of *The Wind in the Willows*](https://newrepublic.com/article/90525/poetry-england-philip-larkin) as a Christmas present early in their relationship, and the two of them made a private world out of it — Grahame and Beatrix Potter both, offering, as one reviewer of their letters puts it, "a ready-made escapist world when their adult relationship becomes too difficult." Larkin signed himself her rabbit, sketched her as an aproned rabbit in the margins, called her his "dearest bun," and admitted once that when they actually met in person he would "grow stiff & silent, and never move off the ground of rabbithood."

That is the book, and roughly the frame of mind, "Days" turns out to have borrowed its ending from — a private refuge Monica had handed him, mined without his noticing for the image of professional death arriving at a run. He wrote the poem for her, described it to her as barely a poem, and it took him eighteen years to tell her, in another letter, where its best line had actually been hiding.

sections.heading: Second-Hand Parts
sections.body:
None of this is available to a reader who only has the ten lines. "Days" reads like something arrived at, not assembled — a question posed and then, in four lines, answered so completely that the poem has nothing left to add. That finality is presumably why David Nicholls printed the whole poem, unedited, as the epigraph to his 2009 novel *One Day*, a book built entirely around the idea that a single date can hold a whole relationship. The poem gets quoted as though it were bedrock.

It isn't. It is a rewritten line grafted onto a childhood memory the poet didn't recognise as a memory until he stumbled back into its source by chance. The priest and the doctor "in their long coats / Running over the fields" feel inevitable, the one truly ominous image in an otherwise plain, chatty poem — and they got there by accident, borrowed from a scene about a stolen car and a pond, understood by their own author only in hindsight. A poem about how days arrive and cannot be questioned too closely turned out to have been built the same way: pieced together first, understood only afterwards.
